article.overview: A hazard avoidance system is a landing-guidance function that finds a safe touchdown spot while a spacecraft is still descending. It uses onboard sensors, usually lidar or cameras, to map the terrain below, identify rocks, craters and steep slopes, and steer the lander toward a site that is clear of them. Unlike a scientific instrument, its purpose is to protect the mission itself: a lander that tips over or lands in a crater can end the mission before any science is returned.
article.description: Hazard avoidance is a capability rather than a single standard device. In the examples documented in this article, it consists of three elements working together: (1) terrain sensing, in which a sensor, typically a lidar (laser ranging) or a camera, builds a three-dimensional map of the surface during descent; (2) hazard analysis, in which software converts the map into quantities such as slope, roughness and the presence of obstacles, then combines them into a cost map that ranks candidate landing sites; and (3) guidance response, in which the guidance system selects a safe target and, if necessary, flies the lander sideways to reach it. NASA's Autonomous Landing and Hazard Avoidance Technology (ALHAT) project describes the same chain: a high-resolution three-dimensional terrain map is generated during the approach trajectory to identify safe landing targets, and its hazard detection and avoidance function works alongside terrain-relative navigation, which compares onboard reconnaissance data with live terrain imagery to refine the spacecraft's position estimate. The ALHAT hazard detection pipeline figure published on the JPL ALHAT page shows terrain, roughness, slope, cost and safe-landing maps for hazard detection and site selection, plus velocity estimation and surface-relative position estimation from lidar scans.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The primary purpose of a hazard avoidance system is to make a landing survivable and precise. Safe touchdown: detecting boulders, craters and slopes steeper than a lander can tolerate reduces the risk of tipping, leg damage or loss of the mission. Precision landing near a target: NASA's ALHAT project states that future lunar missions will need to land near specific resources, which may lie in hazardous terrain, and hazard avoidance is what makes that possible without requiring a perfectly flat site. Enabling more ambitious sites: surface missions that would otherwise be limited to smooth regions can, in principle, target more scientifically interesting terrain. This is a stated design motivation rather than a demonstrated outcome.
article.operating_principle: A hazard avoidance system works during the final part of descent, when the lander is close enough to the surface for its sensors to resolve rocks and craters. Mapping: a flash lidar, which captures a full frame of range measurements at once, or a camera images the surface. In the Morpheus/ALHAT flight tests the flash lidar pointed at the hazard field and built a mosaic of three-dimensional range images, which were combined into a terrain map. Classification: software assesses each map cell for slope and roughness and marks cells that exceed limits; a cost map then favours sites that are flat, clear of obstacles and reachable with the remaining fuel. Target selection and guidance: the guidance system chooses a landing point and, if the nominal target is unsafe, is steered laterally toward the chosen safe site. Navigation support: separate lidars measure velocity and altitude relative to the surface. In the ALHAT design, two lidar scans are aligned to estimate surface-relative velocity, and a small lidar scan is aligned with a larger topographic map to estimate the lander's position relative to the landing site. Human-piloted landings used a similar logic. During Apollo 11, the crew saw that the planned site was rocky and the commander took manual control of the lunar module to fly over it toward a safer area.
article.scientific_importance: Hazard avoidance is not an instrument for measuring the Moon, but it determines which places can be explored. A system that can select safe sites in real time broadens the range of accessible terrain and reduces reliance on pre-mapped, smooth landing regions. Its scientific importance therefore lies in the access it enables.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a hazard avoidance system. Its mass, size, power and performance depend on the sensors, processors and guidance architecture chosen, and on whether the system is an engineering prototype, a flight test article or hardware on a landing mission. The examples below are described by their status and by the values the sources actually state. Where a value is not published in the sources reviewed, this article says so rather than estimating it. The examples differ in purpose, sensor type and status, so their values are not directly comparable and no unified comparison table is given.

examples.name: ALHAT hazard detection sensor suite (Morpheus flight tests)
examples.type: Flight-tested engineering prototype (Earth-based; not a lunar mission)
examples.status: Flown on the Morpheus prototype lander at Kennedy Space Center in 2014. Not flown on the Moon.
examples.project_context: ALHAT was a NASA technology project led by the Johnson Space Center with the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Langley Research Center and Charles Stark Draper Laboratory.

sensor_specifications_as_reported.source_note: Values as reported in the NTRS record summary for Roback et al. (AIAA SciTech 2015). The full PDF could not be parsed; verify against the paper before reuse.

flash_lidar.hazard_identification_stated: Can identify a 30 cm hazard from a 1 km slant range according to the stated sensor performance.

navigation_doppler_lidar.min_operating_range: Down to several metres above ground.

examples.flight_test_results: The flash lidar identified hazards as small as 30 cm from the maximum slant range Morpheus could provide, which was 450 m. Its performance was occasionally degraded by range noise from rocket-heated air, and it was susceptible to pre-triggering on a dust cloud raised at launch. The Doppler lidar met expected accuracy but its signal degraded in heated air. The laser altimeter showed signal attenuation lasting a few seconds from the engine's heat plume.
examples.flight_test_context: Launch from a pad at the Kennedy Space Center Shuttle Landing Facility runway; lunar-like descent from 250 m altitude; landing on a field of rocks, craters and slopes, with safe sites 400 m downrange. The NASA image article describes the 28 May 2014 night free-flight test as 98 seconds long, climbing more than 800 feet and landing about a quarter mile from the launch point.
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions, power and complete suite specifications are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Goddard Hazard Detection Lidar (NASA SPLICE project)
examples.type: Prototype lidar, field-tested from a helicopter (not a lunar mission)
examples.status: Tested from a helicopter at the Kennedy Space Center Shuttle Landing Facility in March 2025. NASA states that additional suborbital flight tests are planned through 2026.
examples.project_context: SPLICE (Safe and Precise Landing - Integrated Capabilities Evolution) is a NASA project that includes a navigation Doppler lidar, terrain-relative navigation, a hazard detection lidar and a descent and landing computer. The hazard detection lidar was developed by the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory for SPLICE according to a NASA overview.

performance_as_reported.mapping_rate: NASA states that the lidar can map an area equivalent to two football fields in two seconds.
performance_as_reported.official_lunar_landing_requirement: Land within 50 metres of the targeted site. This is a requirement, not a demonstrated result.
performance_as_reported.test_outcome: NASA reports that primary flight test objectives were achieved on the first day of testing and that the data confirmed the sensor's capability in a challenging, vibration-heavy environment. The review of the hazard-field terrain reconstruction is described as preliminary. The article does not state that the 50 m requirement was met.

examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions, power and detailed sensor performance (for example range, field of view or frame rate) are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-3 Lander Hazard Detection and Avoidance Camera (LHDAC)
examples.type: Flown lander camera on a lunar landing mission (Chandrayaan-3, 2023)
examples.status: The Vikram lander touched down on the lunar southern polar region on 23 August 2023, according to eoPortal. The mission is described as meeting its objectives.
examples.function: The eoPortal page lists LHDAC among the lander's descent-guidance sensors but does not describe its function, resolution, field of view or mass. Press coverage around the launch describes it as a camera that helps the lander identify a hazard-free site, such as one without boulders or deep trenches, during descent. That description has not been confirmed against a primary ISRO technical source.
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions, power and performance for LHDAC are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Its performance during the actual landing has not been established from the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Apollo 11 crew-piloted hazard avoidance (historical reference)
examples.type: Crew-operated manual control during a lunar landing (not a standalone payload)
examples.status: Flown on Apollo 11 in July 1969. The sources reviewed describe manual control and landing radar rather than an automated hazard detection sensor.
examples.event_summary: The Apollo Lunar Surface Journal records that at 102:43:22 mission elapsed time, Commander Neil Armstrong took manual control and went into program P66 after the planned site proved rocky. Aldrin's callouts put the altitude near 540 feet and then 400 feet during the transition. The editorial note attributes about 0.6 km of the landing overshoot to the manual flying. Post-flight analysis indicated that about 770 pounds of propellant remained, of which about 100 pounds was unusable. Propellant gauge callouts during descent were unreliable because of sloshing, according to the Journal's editorial notes. The radar lost track of the surface twice after manual takeover.
examples.qualification: Not applicable: this was crew-operated equipment and procedure, not a standalone payload.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a hazard avoidance system. The examples differ: the ALHAT and Goddard systems are sensor suites or instruments whose enclosure sizes are not published in the sources reviewed; the Chandrayaan-3 LHDAC is a lander camera whose dimensions are not published in the sources reviewed; and the Apollo 11 case is crew-operated procedure rather than hardware. A new hazard avoidance system would need its dimensions set by its sensor field of view, mounting geometry and the lander's descent configuration.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass for the ALHAT suite, the Goddard Hazard Detection Lidar and the Chandrayaan-3 LHDAC is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, so no mass values are given. Mass affects launch requirements and lander margins, and a sensor suite's mass must be assessed against the lander's descent budget once the design is known.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power for the ALHAT suite, the Goddard Hazard Detection Lidar and the Chandrayaan-3 LHDAC is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The hazard sensors draw power from the lander and must have a data path to the guidance computer. Interface details for a specific lander are not published in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar hazard avoidance system must work in an environment without an atmosphere, with strong illumination changes, dusty surfaces and rapid changes in range during descent. Sensors must tolerate the thermal and mechanical loads of the lander and be protected from the exhaust plume when the engine is firing. The Morpheus tests provide evidence about plume effects: heated air from the engine degraded flash lidar range accuracy by adding scintillation noise, interfered with the Doppler lidar signal and attenuated the laser altimeter for a few seconds, and dust raised by launch caused pre-triggering of the flash lidar during hazard-relative navigation. These observations come from Earth-based prototype flights, so their direct transfer to the lunar environment is not established. The system must also process sensor data, build maps and issue guidance commands within the time available during descent. The NASA SPLICE article reports that the hazard detection lidar can map a large area in about two seconds, but it does not give the required processing latency.
article.limitations: Sensing range and timing: a hazard can only be avoided if it is detected early enough for the lander to change course; the Morpheus flash lidar detected small hazards only at the range it could reach, and many of its useful measurements were degraded by plume effects. Dependence on prior knowledge: hazard detection cannot see beyond the lidar or camera field of view, and terrain-relative navigation and prior maps are often used together with the hazard sensor, which this article does not assess in detail. Fuel margin: a lateral manoeuvre to a safe site consumes propellant, and the limit of any avoidance manoeuvre depends on the lander's design. Performance is not uniform across examples: the sources do not provide comparable accuracy figures for all examples.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A hazard avoidance system is usually a set of sensors and guidance software rather than a separately deployed device. It is therefore integrated into the descent and landing architecture of a lander.
transportation_process: Earth integration: sensors must be mounted with clear fields of view toward the surface, aligned to the vehicle's navigation frame and tested in the lander's electrical and thermal environment.

Launch and transfer: the lidar or camera must survive launch vibration, shock and thermal cycling. The SPLICE field test reported that the sensor's data were good in a vibration-heavy environment, but this is a helicopter test, not a launch qualification.
Landing and deployment: the system is active only during descent and landing. It does not require separate deployment on the surface.
Interfaces: the hazard sensor needs a data path to the guidance computer and power from the lander. Interface details for a specific lander are not published in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable as a separately deployed device. The hazard avoidance function is active during descent and landing and is integrated into the lander's guidance, navigation and control system.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 11 (1969): crew-piloted hazard avoidance with manual takeover of the lunar module during the final descent. Morpheus/ALHAT (2014): Earth-based closed-loop flight tests of a lidar hazard detection system. SPLICE (2025): helicopter field test of the hazard detection lidar. Chandrayaan-3 (2023): LHDAC listed among the lander's descent-guidance sensors.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, including Artemis, is asserted. NASA states that the SPLICE descent and landing computer design is being evaluated for potential avionics upgrades on Artemis systems, but it does not describe a flight plan for the hazard detection lidar on any Artemis mission. Compatibility with a specific lander would need to be assessed against verified interface, mass, power and mounting data, none of which are published in the sources reviewed.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 11 landing showed crew-piloted hazard avoidance in practice. The ALHAT project then matured lidar-based hazard detection and terrain-relative navigation through ground and flight tests. Its Morpheus flights in 2014 were the first in-flight use of three lidar sensors to scan a lunar-like hazard field, identify a safe landing site and guide the lander there. The SPLICE project carried this work forward, and Chandrayaan-3's LHDAC is the sensor in this article that has flown on a lunar landing mission.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No universal specification: the hazard avoidance category includes very different systems, so a single mass, power or accuracy figure would be misleading. Prototype versus flown: ALHAT and SPLICE hardware were tested on Earth; only Chandrayaan-3 LHDAC and the Apollo 11 manual landing involved an actual lunar landing, and the sources do not give the performance of LHDAC during its descent. Chandrayaan-3 function: the purpose of LHDAC as described in press coverage is not confirmed by a primary technical source reviewed here. Sensor values from a summary: the Morpheus sensor values are taken from the NTRS record summary, not a parsed full PDF, and need verification. Missing detail: mass, power, field of view and processing latency for the examples are not published in the sources reviewed. Apollo mission times and fuel figures are from the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal's editorial notes; the propellant readings were unreliable during descent and the post-flight figure is an estimate. Image credits: the JPL diagram and the ALHAT page do not state a photo credit.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Chandrayaan-3 LHDAC: eoPortal confirms only that LHDAC is among the lander's descent-guidance sensors. Its function as described in press coverage (choosing a hazard-free site during descent) is not confirmed by a primary ISRO technical source. Its performance during landing is not established.

Chandrayaan-3: the ISRO landing brochure was not retrievable (HTTP 404), so no primary ISRO document was reviewed. A press-reported lateral hazard-avoidance range was not included because its primary source could not be verified.

Morpheus/ALHAT sensor values come from the NTRS record summary for Roback et al. The full PDF could not be parsed, so these values need checking against the paper. The paper's 1 km flash lidar hazard-identification value and the 450 m maximum test slant range both appear and are presented in context; they are different quantities.

ALHAT JPL page: no flight history, performance figures or requirements appear on the page. Earlier secondary search results mentioned a 3-sigma 90 m requirement, a 3 m local precision requirement and a 2014 Free Flight 11 date; these were not verified against a primary source and are excluded from the article.

Apollo 11: times, altitudes, downrange overshoot and fuel figures are from the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal editorial notes. The post-flight propellant figure is an estimate. A downrange manual-flying distance from a search snippet of the Apollo 11 Mission Report was not verified and is excluded. The Apollo 11 Mission Report PDF exceeded the fetch size limit.
Apollo 11 radar: a museum-record description of a continuous wave Doppler radar was seen in search results only and is not included in the article.

SPLICE/Goddard hazard detection lidar: NASA states a 50 m landing requirement and two-second mapping of an area equivalent to two football fields. Mass, dimensions, power and detailed sensor specifications are not published in the sources reviewed.
Image credit: the JPL ALHAT pipeline diagram does not state a credit. The NASA Morpheus and SPLICE images carry NASA credits. Usage and reuse conditions have not been checked for any image.

Images not included: the SPLICE test team photograph and descent and landing computer preparation photograph were found and returned HTTP 200 but were not visually reviewed, so they are not included in the article.
Full-resolution downloads were not checked for any image. The JPL diagram was reviewed at its 1000x500 rendition.
Landing-site coordinates for Chandrayaan-3 appear in eoPortal but were intentionally not included, because the article does not make landing-site recommendations.
No lander compatibility, Artemis flight assignment or flight-proven status for ALHAT, SPLICE or the Goddard lidar is asserted; the sources reviewed do not verify these.
